summary: Gives a methodology for benchmarking local area network (LAN) switching devices. It describes how to run tests so results can be compared. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: This is a recipe for testing how fast network switches really are, so everybody measures them the same way.

subtitle: A structured approach to testing LAN switch performance.

tldr.problem: LAN switching devices vary widely in performance, but there was no standard way to benchmark and compare them fairly.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2889 defines a set of test procedures with specific traffic patterns, frame sizes, and metrics so vendors and users can measure switch behavior consistently.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can now evaluate switches using comparable metrics: throughput, frame loss, forwarding rate, address caching, and other characteristics.

today: RFC 2889 is an Informational RFC defining the methodology and remains the standard approach for benchmarking LAN switching devices. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2889 extends the general benchmarking methodology from RFC 2544 to the specific domain of LAN switching devices. The RFC focuses on devices that switch frames at the MAC (Media Access Control) layer, which is where most Ethernet switches operate. It provides methodology for benchmarking switching devices on forwarding performance, congestion control, latency, address handling and filtering.

The document explicitly adopts RFC 2119 language: MUST, SHOULD, MAY terms carry specific meanings about what is required, recommended or optional when running these tests.
sections.eli5: This is the instruction manual for testing how fast a network switch can send data, whether it drops frames, and if it correctly learns MAC addresses.

sections.title: Test Setup and Prerequisites
sections.content:
Before running tests, the RFC requires that the Device Under Test (DUT) learn MAC addresses that will be used in testing. This address learning must be verified before each test run, as unlearned addresses cause the switch to flood frames instead of forwarding them correctly, corrupting the results.

The RFC also addresses a practical problem: switches that use hashing algorithms for address learning may fail to learn the specific addresses needed for tests. To handle this, the test frame format must allow MAC addresses to be rearranged so the switch can learn them all.

Frame formats support three types of Ethernet frames: standard untagged frames, frames with vendor-specific tags, and IEEE 802.3ac tagged frames for 802.1p and 802.1Q. Some tagged frames exceed the standard 1518-byte maximum and may not be accepted by all switches.
sections.eli5: Before measuring, you need to teach the switch which addresses matter, and pick the right type of test frames so the switch can understand them.

sections.title: Core Benchmarking Tests
sections.content:
RFC 2889 defines ten specific tests, each with a clear objective, setup parameters, procedure, measurements and reporting format.

Fully meshed throughput tests the switch when all ports send and receive traffic to and from all other ports simultaneously, measuring maximum throughput at zero frame loss. Partially meshed tests use traffic patterns where some ports act only as senders while others receive (one-to-many, many-to-one, multiple devices with backbone uplink).

Congestion control tests determine if the switch implements proper flow control and whether congestion on one port affects traffic to uncongested ports (Head-of-Line Blocking versus Backpressure). Forward pressure tests measure the highest forwarding rate and detect violations of the minimum interframe gap when the switch is overloaded.

Address caching capacity uses a binary search algorithm to find the exact number of MAC addresses the switch can learn. Address learning rate measures how quickly new addresses are learned. Error filtering tests whether the switch correctly filters invalid frames (CRC errors, oversize, undersize, dribble bits, alignment errors).

Broadcast forwarding and latency measures how the switch handles frames sent to all ports simultaneously, including both throughput and individual frame latency to each destination.
sections.eli5: These tests check: can it handle all ports talking at once? What happens when one port is overwhelmed? How many addresses does it remember? Does it catch bad frames?

sections.title: Key Metrics and Reporting
sections.content:
The RFC defines specific metrics to measure and report.

Throughput is the maximum offered load with zero frame loss, found via a search algorithm that adjusts the input load.

Forwarding Rate (FR) is the number of test frames per second successfully forwarded to the correct destination at a specified offered load. Maximum Forwarding Rate (MFR) is the peak forwarding rate across all offered load levels. Forwarding Rate at Maximum Offered Load (FRMOL) is the rate at the device's maximum capacity.

Frame loss rate measures the percentage of transmitted frames that do not arrive at the correct destination. This is reported at the end of a test trial duration (typically 30 seconds).

Each test specifies setup parameters: frame sizes (recommended: 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 1280, 1518 bytes), interframe gap, duplex mode, intended load as a percentage of medium's theoretical maximum, burst size, number of addresses per port, and trial duration. Results should be reported as graphs comparing theoretical and actual performance across different frame sizes.
sections.eli5: These are the numbers to measure: how many frames got through per second, how many got lost, and how it compares to what physics says should happen.

sections.title: Practical Testing Challenges
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges several real-world complications in switch testing.

Switches often generate their own frames (spanning tree, SNMP, RIP) that must not be counted as received test frames. The test frame format includes a unique signature field to identify test frames and filter out device-generated or misforwarded frames.

When testing with multiple addresses per port, the RFC specifies that source and destination address pairs should be chosen randomly to properly exercise the switch's address lookup capability.

The address aging time of the switch must be configured sufficiently long that learned addresses do not age out during the test, or results will show artificially low performance. Similarly, burst transmission must be carefully managed: all ports should start transmitting within 1% of the trial duration to avoid timing artifacts.

For congestion control testing, the RFC must be run with the exact traffic distribution algorithm specified (round-robin order) to maintain balance and avoid skewing results toward particular ports or causing artificial blocking.
sections.eli5: Real testing is tricky: the switch creates its own traffic, addresses age out, timing matters, and you have to test exactly as specified or results don't mean anything.
